findings.input: new ForeignTokenRegistry([{ name: "acme", pattern: /ACME_[A-Z0-9_]+/g }]).namespaceOf("ACME_ABCDEF_0001") called repeatedly
findings.config: foreign registry with a pattern-registered namespace whose RegExp carries the g (or y) flag
findings.expected_invariant: The same registration must yield the same ownership verdict on every call, and classifyOwnership / ctx.isProtectedToken / the forward path must agree with each other. Registry contract: a registered foreign token is PRESERVED on the input path.
findings.observed: namespaceOf alternates acme/null/acme/null because RegExp.prototype.test on a g or y matcher advances lastIndex; classifyOwnership resets lastIndex before matching while isProtectedToken does not, so the two layers fight over one matcher object. Consequence: DB_PASSWORD=ACME_ABCDEF_0001 is redacted to DB_PASSWORD=CRG_... instead of being preserved, and the verdict depends on call order.
findings.impact: ownership/policy inconsistency + deployment correctness. A shared registry built once at startup gives different results than one built per request. No confidentiality leak: the failure direction is over-redaction. An EXACT registration is unaffected.
findings.control: an equivalent non-stateful matcher (/ACME_[A-Z0-9_]+/) preserves the token correctly, which locates the defect in how the matcher is used rather than in the registry's purpose
findings.root_cause: normalizeForeignNamespace kept the caller's RegExp object unchanged and namespaceOf called .test() directly. On a g or y matcher .test() advances lastIndex, so the same token alternated between FOREIGN_REGISTERED and UNKNOWN; classifyOwnership reset lastIndex before matching while isProtectedToken did not, so the two layers fought over one shared matcher object and the verdict depended on call order.
findings.fix: Two layers. (1) normalizeForeignNamespace clones: new RegExp(pattern.source, pattern.flags), so neither side can observe the other's cursor. (2) A single namespaceMatches(matcher, value) helper resets lastIndex to 0 before the call and fixes it back to 0 in a finally block; namespaceFindAll does the same for the three String.match enumeration sites. Deliberately not 'save and restore the old value': a registry-internal matcher should not carry observable cursor state at all, so 0 is the honest end state.
findings.regression: test/adversarial/registry.test.js -- 100-call stability, cross-layer agreement, forward-path preservation, call-order independence (A,B,A,B,A vs A,A,A,B,B), caller-regex isolation in both directions, reusable-registry stability, exact-registration immunity, and every matcher shape.

findings.input: registry with { name: "acme", pattern: /ACME_[A-Z0-9_]+/y }; applySinkPolicy("curl x?y=ACME_ABCDEF_0001", ctx, { kind: "tool_argument" })
findings.config: foreign registry whose namespace matcher carries the sticky flag y
findings.expected_invariant: Ownership recognition must not depend on WHERE in a document a token appears. A registered foreign token that is protected in prose must also be protected as an operand, or the two channels disagree for one registration.
findings.observed: A sticky matcher only matches at lastIndex 0. namespaceOf calls .test() with the cursor at 0, and namespaceFindAll uses String.match which with y is anchored at lastIndex as well, so the registry cannot FIND a token that has anything before it. Result for one registration: namespaceOf("ACME_ABCDEF_0001") = acme and isProtectedToken = true, while inside "curl x?y=ACME_ABCDEF_0001" namespaceOf = null and an untrusted tool operand is DELIVERED instead of refused.
findings.impact: ownership/policy inconsistency between the prose channel and the operand channel for sticky registrations. No plaintext is exposed: the failure direction is that this layer hands over a token it cannot resolve, which the outer DLP owns. Severity Low, and only reachable with a sticky matcher, which the design does not recommend but does accept.
findings.reproduce: node --test test/adversarial/registry.test.js (test 'R2-REG OBSERVATION: a STICKY matcher cannot find a token mid-document')
findings.control: the equivalent /g matcher refuses the operand, which is the expected behaviour
findings.relationship: INDEPENDENT of R2-REG-001. Verified by stashing the stateful-matcher fix and re-running: the behaviour above is identical before and after, so it is pre-existing and was neither caused nor cured by that fix. Deliberately NOT folded into R2-REG-001, per the rule that several red points are usually not one root cause.
findings.fix: namespaceFindAll is now a real DOCUMENT SEARCH while namespaceOf keeps the matcher's declared semantics unchanged. The scan runs on a clone with y removed and g ensured, and every candidate it proposes is re-checked against the ORIGINAL matcher, so discovery is not authority and the registry's own matcher is never permanently rewritten. namespaceOf(TOKEN) = acme and namespaceOf(prefix + TOKEN) = null are both unchanged for a sticky matcher.
findings.regression: test/adversarial/registry.test.js -- membership unchanged in both directions for sticky; the operand is now refused; prose still preserves; the registry keeps its declared flags; every flag combination scans AND keeps its membership semantics (only y/gy are anchored, corrected from an earlier table that wrongly expected gi to be anchored); and admission is not widened, asserted on classifyOwnership rather than on a span, with a case-sensitivity control.

findings.input:
A=cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM0NTY3OA==   (minimal)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
data:
  a: cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM0NTY3OA==
  b: cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM0NTY3OA==   (K8s path)
findings.expected_invariant: The replacement is self-delimiting: a redaction replaces a whole value and leaves NO characters of the original beside it. R1 already pins that every emitted token matches ^CRG_[A-Z0-9]{4,}_[A-Z0-9]{4,}$ and that no truncated PREFIX survives; the converse -- a complete replacement with leftover characters glued to it -- is the uncovered half.
findings.observed: The entropy detector's span stops before base64 padding, so the padding survives next to the replacement. Minimal: `A=cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM0NTY3OA==` becomes `A=CRG_AAAAAA_0001==`, and the single-padding form becomes `A=CRG_AAAAAA_0001=`. In a K8s Secret the two occurrences of one plaintext produce two spans that differ by the padding -- gitleaks takes the padded form, entropy the unpadded one -- which overlap WITHOUT containment, so the merge keeps both and the second yields `b: Q1JHX0FBQUFBQV8wMDAy==`, a base64 encode of a second token with the ORIGINAL padding appended. Two occurrences of one plaintext therefore get two different replacements.
findings.impact: Integrity and representation correctness, in every context rather than only K8s: the emitted value is neither the replacement nor the original, `CRG_AAAAAA_0001==` is not a token and is not valid base64 either, and one plaintext acquires two identities. Round-trip happens to survive because the residual `==` is still the original's padding and restoration is substring-based -- asserted, so the claim is exact. No confidentiality fail-open was found.
findings.verified_pre_existing: Confirmed with `git stash` that the behaviour is identical with and without the R2-REG-001/R2-REG-002 fixes, so it is not related to those.
findings.why_r1_missed_it: R1's token-shape property removes every full token and then checks that no `CRG_` PREFIX remains. Residue that sits AFTER a complete token is invisible to that check, so the property only covered truncation, not trailing leftovers.
findings.root_cause: tokenizeBlocks() scores runs of [A-Za-z0-9]+ for entropy, so the EVIDENCE for a base64 scalar covers the core and stops before the padding. The consequence was 'one plaintext, two identities', but that is NOT a ledger defect: the raw strings handed to the mapping genuinely differed (occurrence 1 raw = padded form, occurrence 2 raw = unpadded form), so rawToToken legitimately allocated two identities. The chain is: entropy boundary truncation -> original representation residue survives -> the second occurrence's raw differs -> the mapping allocates a second identity, exactly as its contract says. The real defect is that detector evidence boundary != representation mutation boundary: the detector had already shown the core was worth protecting, but nothing treated the trailing `=` as part of the ENCODED SCALAR.
findings.fix: A narrow base64 REPRESENTATION envelope, alongside the existing reference and infra envelopes: the detector keeps the verdict, the representation supplies the boundary. base64ScalarAt() widens an evidence span by at most the padding bytes and only when the result is a complete canonical base64 scalar that STARTS where the span starts, ends at the scalar's end, has at most two padding characters, and decodes to printable text. classifiedText keeps the original detector core, so widening does not change the classification input -- the same rule the reference envelope follows. Deliberately NOT done: extending the entropy alphabet to include `=` (that pollutes the scoring model to solve a representation problem and moves every score), and a merge special case for entropy+gitleaks overlap (that would teach the geometry layer to parse base64 syntax).
findings.regression: test/adversarial/representation.test.js -- the emitted VALUE (extracted as the RHS, since the assignment's own `=` makes a whole-line search meaningless) must be exactly one complete token; every occurrence's boundary must cover the full encoded scalar; a K8s value must be canonical base64 AND ledger-owned AND resolve to an owned token; the same raw must no longer split into two identities; classification input stays the detector core; the matrix over env/yaml/k8s x H/G/H+G x no-padding/one-=/two-==; three occurrences sharing one identity. Negative controls: an `==` operator after a high-entropy run is not swallowed; a non-canonical, mis-positioned, over-padded or alphabet-continued candidate is not widened; and a canonical scalar IS widened, so the controls are not vacuous.
findings.oracle_corrections: Two regression oracles were wrong before the fix and were corrected first. (1) `out.includes(residue)` can never pass for residue '=' because the assignment itself contains '='; the value is now extracted and asserted to be a complete token. For the non-canonical single-'=' input the honest outcome is the token followed by the stray character, which is asserted explicitly. (2) The old test pinned the bug's shape with `assert.deepEqual(covered, [B64, B64.slice(0, -2)])`, which would fail the moment the implementation became correct; it now asserts the contract that each boundary covers the complete encoded scalar. Also measured: with `G only` the gitleaks rule does not fire on this blob because it gates on its own entropy check, so 'no padding survives' only applies once something was actually redacted.
